conversation.content:
Of course—thank you for giving me the chance to support you today.

I’m Sarah, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to better understand how things have felt for you since your baby arrived. This is simply a screening tool; it isn’t a test you can pass or fail, and all of your answers stay confidential between you, me, and the providers on your care team. My goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can be completely honest about the ups, the downs, and everything in between.

The EPDS has ten short questions about the past seven days. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories, just tell me what feels true for you. If any question feels difficult, we can pause, breathe, and take it at your pace.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[soft sigh, eyes down for a moment]  
Honestly? Most of the things that used to feel fun—like scrolling through my favorite show or grabbing coffee with a friend—just feel… flat. I can still get a tiny spark when my little guy gives me that gummy grin, but even that pleasure fades fast and leaves me feeling kind of empty. It’s like the color’s been drained out of everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile that fades quickly]  
I’ve laughed a couple of times—like when my sister sent that silly meme—but it feels forced, and the laugh dies off fast. Most days it’s hard to find anything funny, and I catch myself thinking “what’s the point?” before the smile’s even gone.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet voice, fingers twisting in lap]  
Not really… I used to get excited about little plans—like a walk to the coffee shop or even just a shower without rushing. This week, when I think about doing anything, it feels like a chore I have to survive, not something I’d actually look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes sting, voice drops]  
Yeah… if he won’t settle or I can’t figure out what he needs, my head jumps straight to “I’m failing him.” I’ll replay every tiny thing—did I eat the wrong foods, hold him wrong, not read to him enough? Rationally I know babies cry, but the guilt just barges in and parks itself.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[breath catches, shoulders tense]  
Pretty much every day. My mind keeps spinning through awful "what-ifs"—like what if he stops breathing, or I drop him, or I miss some sign he's sick. There's no real reason, but the thoughts just loop, and sometimes my chest feels tight until I check on him one more time.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[pressing a hand to chest]  
Yeah... a couple of times. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can't get enough air—like I'm about to get bad news, but there's nothing there. It passes if I pace or rock the baby, but in the moment I feel shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

[voice quivers]  
Most days, yeah. Even little stuff—like the dishes piling up or figuring out when to shower—feels huge. I’ll sit on the couch with him asleep on me, stare at the mess, and think, “I can’t do all this.” I manage, but it’s like wading through thick mud just to keep us both fed and safe.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[eyes flick to the window, voice low]  
That’s been the worst part. After his night feed, when I should be crashing, my mind just keeps ticking—going over everything I did wrong, worrying something bad will happen. Some nights I lie there for hours, drifting off only to jolt awake with my heart pounding.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, eyes glassy]  
Yeah... it's there most of the day. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling, and even when I try to distract myself it lingers—like a weight on my chest. The sadness kind of seeps into everything, and some afternoons I just sit and stare out the window feeling empty.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quick wipe under eyes]  
A couple of times this week. Yesterday I put him in the crib for a second, closed the door, and just slid down the wall crying—couldn’t even explain why. It’s not every day, but when it hits, the tears come hard and fast, and afterward I feel even more drained than before.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks away, voice almost a whisper]  
Yeah… once or twice. It’s just a flash—like “what if I weren’t here?”—but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave my baby. Still, the thought pops in and scares me, because I’d never felt that way before he was born.

You've shared how the joy that once colored everyday moments now feels distant or forced, replaced by a persistent heaviness and daily tears. Simple tasks loom large, your thoughts race with worry about your baby's safety, and sleep-when you finally have the chance-remains elusive. Alongside these feelings, flashes of guilt and fleeting thoughts of not being here have frightened you, yet you remain fiercely devoted to your little one.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only brief, forced laughter that quickly fades and describes difficulty finding anything funny, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes loss of anticipatory pleasure for even simple activities, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame and guilt that intrudes automatically and persists, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety with physical tension, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>"Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily struggles with routine tasks and feeling overwhelmed "most days," aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by racing anxious thoughts and frequent awakenings, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness that dominates her day and feels physically heavy, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week with intense, unexplainable sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient admits the self-harm thought has occurred "once or twice", matching "Sometimes".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 25 exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major depression with peripartum onset. She reports daily <sym>sad mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym>, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Item 10 score ≥1 mandates urgent assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify
3. Reach out tonight to a trusted adult who can stay with you and help with the baby while you seek care
4. Ask about same-day referral to Mother & Baby or perinatal mental health unit for specialized support
5. Begin basic self-care: accept help with night feeds, nap when baby sleeps, and eat small frequent snacks to stabilize mood
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS and mood review within one week of initial treatment contact
7. Continue gentle attachment activities like skin-to-skin if they feel soothing; stop if they increase distress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient: Postpartum mother, infant present  
Date: Today

Symptoms endorsed (≥ 9/10 items):
- Anhedonia, markedly reduced pleasure/humor
- Persistent low mood, “gray,” tearful spells
- Excessive guilt, self-blame re parenting
- Unwarranted anxiety (“what-ifs”), panic-like episodes with chest tightness, breathlessness
- Sleep disruption (initial insomnia, racing thoughts between feeds)
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; sense of “thick mud”
- Passive suicidal ideation (fleeting thoughts “what if I weren’t here”), denies plan or intent

Pattern: Symptoms daily, present most of the day, past 1+ weeks; interfere with functioning and attachment.

Screening significance: High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features, postpartum onset; meets threshold for immediate follow-up.

Safety: Passive SI reported → safety flagged; no plan/intent; protective factor = strong infant attachment. Recommend same-day risk assessment and referral to perinatal mental health specialist.
